summary:
Lakshadweep stands under India's national framework. As a union territory without a full legislature, it has no separate trans statute: legal recognition, policing practice and identity-document rules that reach a visitor or resident are set by the central government. No Lakshadweep-specific recognition policy, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

The national baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Recognition narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed by Parliament amends the 2019 law: it removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling, narrows the statutory definition of a transgender person, and limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Human Rights Watch calls the bill a major reversal of the 2014 rights and has urged the president not to sign it; both houses approved the measure and presidential assent was still awaited as of the BBC's reporting.

The amendment mandates medical certification for identity recognition, which bears directly on the documents a trans traveller presents. Critics describe mandatory medical certification as an attack on privacy and dignity. Passport authorities have already required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, and the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

Exclusion is the central criticism. The government says the narrower definition improves delivery of welfare schemes, while critics warn it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people; rights activists describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The government also presents the 2019 framework as protection from trafficking. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 amendment reverses the direction set by the Supreme Court's 2014 recognition of a third gender, so a visitor's expectation rests on two authorities pulling apart: a constitutional ruling that established self-identification and a statute that withdraws it.

Human Rights Watch and the government characterise the same measure differently. One treats it as a major reversal of protected rights and an exclusionary narrowing; the other treats the narrower definition as a way to improve welfare delivery. The disagreement is substantive rather than terminological, and it concerns who is eligible for state schemes as much as who is recognised.

Protection and exposure run in parallel. Decriminalisation in 2018 and high-court intervention in 2021 sit alongside the 2024 removal of gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences and documented abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters in 2024 and 2026. Statutory recognition narrowed while judicial remedies stayed available, which is why contact with police and security personnel is the pressure point rather than the statute alone.

India's trans population is estimated at two million, so the amended definition governs a large domestic constituency, not a marginal category.

For residents, the amended definition determines access to welfare schemes, and the government has presented that narrower definition as improving delivery. People whose gender identity falls outside the historically accepted categories or intersex status are excluded from the recognition scheme and, by extension, from schemes conditioned on it.

Identity documents now depend on medical certification rather than self-declaration. The same requirement has already appeared at the passport stage, where a medical examination was demanded of a trans applicant before the Allahabad High Court intervened in February 2026.

Sexual-violence protection changed with the criminal code. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code in 2024 without the gender-identity-specific offences that had covered trans people, and community reporting points to fear of more assaults under the new provisions.

Policing practice carries both documented harm and court-ordered remedy. The Madras High Court's June 2021 guidelines directed police sensitisation, barred conversion therapy and addressed medical and education authorities, while the UK Home Office's December 2025 note characterised police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and not systemic.
